title: Enemy render cost measured: CPU re-pose is the only thing that fails; merged shader clouds carry 1.38M dots in one call, and the jelly body works at swarm scale
context: Owner is deciding enemy type and rendering so the game can scale to swarms, and wants the cost understood before any decision: per unit, at large scale, and for smooth animation. Open questions were whether the amoeba is too expensive to use widely, why the borrowed roster is 150 dots, whether the jelly-effect boss body could be used for smaller enemies, and whether unexplored options (cheap deforming spheres, shaders, resolution LOD by crowd size) are better. The owner wants to keep the BJJ belt colour ladder, the solid-core tell and the hard-core proximity sensor, which playtested well.
outcome: Measured on an M4 (ANGLE Metal, headless Chrome via scripts/chrome-proc.mjs, vsync-free with gl.finish, median of 60 frames, 1280x720, bare scene). Frame cost in ms at 20/100/500/2000 units: current CPU re-posed cloud 0.30/1.40/6.80/27.50 (23.78 ms of the last is CPU animation alone, 36 fps, the only failing path); static cloud 0/0.10/0.40/1.60; vertex-shader wobble cloud 0/0.10/0.40/1.60, identical to static, so the deformation is free; merged single-draw-call shader cloud under 0.10 at every size, carrying 1,384,000 animated dots in ONE draw call at 2000 amoebas; jelly bodies 0/0.10/0.40/2.00 at 2000, which is 5.6M triangles. Node microbenchmark of the pure functions: waveJelly 13.617 us per amoeba per frame (692 dots, 8.1 KB/frame upload), 8.932 us phage (494), swimWave 5.875 us jellyfish (578); 100 amoebas is 47.5 MB/s of buffer upload against the 99 MB/s that jelly.js already rejected for a single imported boss. Conclusions: dot count is not a cost axis once the wobble leaves the CPU; per-unit CPU re-pose is the whole problem; the jelly body is viable for ordinary enemies, not only bosses; per-instance colour in the merged path makes the belt ladder free at swarm scale; resolution LOD by crowd size is unnecessary for cost on this class of GPU. The 150-dot roster figure was traced to the default parameter of enemyDotPts and an archive note that round 1 is 150 points of fodder, not to any measurement; neighbouring defaults are 170, 190, 400 and 1150. Also found: the phage is the only one of the classic three without its own movement treatment, receiving waveJelly (a blob squash-stretch) on a rigid lunar-lander silhouette, which is the reported bad animation; the jellyfish already has swimWave. DOT_SHAPES can swap a silhouette without touching the type id, as scoutufo and saucer already do, so replacing the phage's shape needs no change to story beats, cinematics, lore or tests.
alternatives: Reduce dot density to buy performance: rejected by measurement, density is not the cost axis once the wobble is on the GPU.
Render at high resolution for small crowds and drop resolution at large ones: available but unnecessary for cost at these sizes; keep for weak devices rather than as an architecture.
Replace dot clouds wholesale with meshes: unnecessary, both idioms are affordable, so representation can be chosen aesthetically.
evidence: Headless benchmark comparing cloud-cpu, cloud-static, cloud-shader, cloud-merged and jelly at 20/100/500/2000; renderer.info for draw calls and primitive counts; gl.finish to defeat vsync (first run read a flat 16.6 ms across every variant, which was vsync, not work).
Node microbenchmark of waveJelly and swimWave over 20,000 iterations after warmup.
src/units.js header claims per-vertex CPU animation does not scale to crowds; measurement confirms the CPU path but shows the same clouds are nearly free once the wobble moves to the vertex shader.
Rendering only. Pathing, collision, hit detection and the hard-core proximity sensor at swarm counts are NOT measured and are the likely remaining ceiling.
